name: Fazao-Malfakassa National Park
blurb: Togo's largest park: savanna, hill forest and antelope, with few predators left.

tip.title: Dry the grass
tip.text: Lower Bluestem grasses to -50% and watch the kob and roan antelope fall, then the leopard and the scavengers that rely on their carcasses.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Seasonal rain drives growth of grasses and forest plants on the hills and in the valleys of the reserve.
Savanna woodland and hilltop grassland in this region burn in the dry season, which renews grass growth and clears dead material.
Soil in the hills and valleys holds the nutrients and moisture that plants draw on.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down dead plants, dung and carcasses and return nutrients to the soil.

nodes.name: Bluestem grasses
nodes.desc: Tall tropical grasses of the savanna. Hyparrhenia is among the grasses kob are known to favour.

nodes.name: Trema
nodes.desc: A fast-growing pioneer tree recorded near the reserve, found in forest edges and clearings where it makes small fruits.

nodes.name: Termites
nodes.desc: Fungus-growing termites that collect plant litter and build mounds. They are a major food for reptiles, birds and other insect-eaters.

nodes.name: Buffon's kob
nodes.desc: A grazing antelope that favours short grass near water. Aerial surveys in the 1980s counted it as the most numerous antelope in the reserve.
A large grass-eating antelope of woodland and savanna; the western subspecies ranges from Senegal to Benin.
Eats grass, browse and fruit and can reshape woodland. Poaching in the 1990s left only a remnant population in the reserve.
Feeds on fruit, flowers and leaves and spreads seeds through forests. Recorded near the reserve.
A widespread songbird that eats fruit and insects. A GloBI record shows black kites taking it.
A forest hornbill, the most recorded bird near the reserve, that eats fruit and insects.
A raptor with double-jointed legs that raids cavity nests for eggs and chicks and also hunts reptiles and insects.
An opportunistic hunter and scavenger. GloBI records show it taking straw-coloured fruit bats and common bulbuls.
An unusual vulture that mostly eats fruit but also takes frogs, insects, small animals and carrion.
A generalist cat that takes medium-sized antelope where they are common. It has become rare across West Africa, so its local status is uncertain.
